title: Arctic Emergency Management Conference 2025 Evaluation Report
text:
This report presents evaluation and recommendations from the Arctic Emergency Management Conference 2025, including evaluation of the overall conference and planning project goals, feedback and recommendations for the thematic sessions. The thematic sessions included community preparedness, health preparedness, marine environmental response, wildland fires, search and rescue, and radiological and nuclear preparedness. In addition, feedback is provided for the two workshops that took place as a part of the conference, the Indigenous Knowledge Mobilization workshop and the Arctic Oil Spill Research and Development Initiative workshop, and poster and science sessions, demonstrations, as well as practical organization of the conference.

This report presents evaluation and 
recommendations from the Arctic Emergency 
Management Conference 2025, including 
evaluation of the overall conference and planning 
project goals, feedback and recommendations 
for the thematic sessions. The thematic sessions 
included community preparedness, health 
preparedness, marine environmental response, 
wildland fires, search and rescue, and radiological 

and nuclear preparedness. In addition, feedback 
is provided for the two workshops that took 
place as a part of the conference, the Indigenous 
Knowledge Mobilization workshop and the Arctic 
Oil Spill Research and Development Initiative 
workshop, and poster and science sessions, 
demonstrations, as well as practical organization 
of the conference.

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 THE ARCTIC EMERGENCY 
MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE
The Arctic Emergency Management Conference 
2025 was held 18-20 March 2025 in Bodø, 
Norway at the Nord University campus, and 
streaming was provided for the first day and 
selected thematic sessions. The conference was 
hosted by the Norwegian Chairship of the Arctic 
Council. The conference organization was led 
by the Arctic Council’s Emergency Prevention, 
Preparedness and Response Working Group’s 
(EPPR) Chair (Norway) supported by EPPR 
Secretariat, in cooperation with Nord University’s 
Center for Crisis Management and Collaboration - 
Nordlab. 

The Arctic Emergency Management Conference 
2025 was part of the official program of the 
Norwegian Chairship of the Arctic Council 
in 2023-2025 and reflects Norway’s goal of 
enhancing Arctic cooperation on these critical 
issues.

More than 200 people from across the Arctic and 
beyond gathered in Bodø, Norway – and over 130 
joined online. Over three days, representatives 
from emergency management services, academia, 
Indigenous Peoples and the Arctic Council hosted 
and engaged in sessions, workshops, poster 
presentations and an exhibition to network, learn 
from each other and advance work on emergency 
management in the Arctic.

The conference was one of the first international 
conferences dedicated to a holistic view of Arctic 
emergency management and provided a platform 
for discussions, information exchange and for 
advancing work. 

7

Morten Høglund, SAO Chair; Photo credit Jessica Cook/Arctic Council Secretariat 

The Emergency Prevention, Preparedness and 
Response Working Group of the Arctic Council 
(EPPR) strives to be the premier international 
forum for collaboration on Arctic emergency 
issues in order to advance risk mitigation and 
improve response capacity and capabilities in 
the Arctic.

EPPR implements projects and activities to 
enhance cooperation, information sharing, data 
collection and addressing gaps in the field of 
Arctic emergencies. EPPR’s main areas of work 
include:

ABOUT EMERGENCY PREVENTION PREPAREDNESS AND 

RESPONSE WORKING GROUP (EPPR)

• Capacity building and improving 
understanding of Arctic emergencies

• Development of guidance and risk 
assessment tools and best practices

• Coordination and preparation of Arctic 
response exercises

• Maintaining and supporting the Agreement 
on Cooperation on Marine Oil Spill 
Preparedness and Response in the Arctic 
(MOSPA Agreement) and the Agreement on 
Cooperation on Aeronautical and Maritime 
Search and Rescue in the Arctic (Arctic SAR 
Agreement).

• Knowledge and information sharing

8 ARCTIC EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE 

ABOUT NORD UNIVERSITY

Nord University is a young university with 
strong regional ties and a global perspective. 
Through research, education and social 
engagement, Nord University contributes 
to the creation of a sustainable future. In 
cooperation with society, business and 
industry in Northern and Central Norway, 
our 11,500 students and 1,350 staff promote 
innovative solutions and knowledge-based 
practice, both locally and internationally. 

Nord University has four strategic focus 
areas: blue and green growth, sustainable 
innovation and entrepreneurship, societal 
security, and health, welfare and education. 
Nord University has an ambition to strengthen 
research within risk assessment, emergency 
preparedness and international development.

Photo: Nord University

The Center for Crisis Management and 
Collaboration contributes to the realization 
of the university's focus area within Societal 
Security. The Center for research, education and 
competence development has a special focus 
within the fields of emergency preparedness, 
exercises and collaboration in the Arctic. At the 
core of the center is Nordlab, an exercise and 
simulator laboratory which offers facilities in 
Bodø for carrying out various types of exercises, 
research, dialogue with emergency response 
actors and dissemination of knowledge.

The Center for Crisis Management and 
Collaboration is organized under the Business 
School. Nord University Business School 
educates tomorrow’s economists, leaders and 
innovators. Through close cooperation with 
business and industry, the public sector and the 
community, Nord University Business School 
provides relevant education and research of an 
international standard. 

9

1.2 CONFERENCE GOALS 

Norwegian Arctic Council Chairship’s overarching goal associated to the conference

Conference goals aligned with the Norwegian Chairship program

To strengthen cooperation on emergency preparedness 
and safe shipping in the Arctic

• Strengthen cooperation on emergency preparedness and safe 
shipping in the Arctic.

• Develop Arctic cooperation on aeronautical and maritime 
search and rescue, oil spill preparedness and response, dealing 
with radiological and nuclear contamination at sea, and health 
preparedness. 

• Identify actions to deal with the environmental problems 
associated with expanding human activity.

• Strengthen the preparedness and cooperation with Arctic 
Indigenous Peoples and local communities for all types of 
emergencies, including wildland fires in Arctic by leveraging local 
and traditional knowledge.

10 ARCTIC EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE 

PROJECT PLAN AT A GLANCE
Project Goals for the Arctic Emergency Management Conference

• Conduct a well-organized conference in 2025 with 250 participants 
with public sector representatives, Indigenous Peoples of the Arctic, 
academia, industry and other relevant organizations.

• Achieve an interesting and well-balanced program by involving 
relevant experts from states and Indigenous Peoples in the planning 
process. 

• Raise awareness about the Arctic Council and the Norwegian 
Chairship 

• Develop a report from the conference including the presented aspects 
of emergency prevention, preparedness and response in the Arctic, 
with recommendations for strengthening emergency management in 
the Arctic.

1.3 ABOUT CONFERENCE PLANNING 
AND ORGANIZATION
Norwegian EPPR Chair developed a project plan 
to guide the planning and organization of the 
conference. A Norwegian stakeholder meeting for 
organizations part of the Norwegian delegation 
to EPPR was first organized in January 2024 to 
establish a content outline for the event, and for 
the process of developing the program committee 
covering major thematic areas through sub-
committees. The planning of the AEMC was 
guided by the identified conference goals with 
the Norwegian Chairship program of the Arctic 
Council as a starting point.

The core organizational team of EPPR Chair and 
secretariat, Nord University representatives and 
ACS communications team (the project group) 
started the work in early 2024 to developed a set 
of guiding documents that were approved by the 
Norwegian Chairship, including a conference 

concept note, project plan, communications 
strategy and risk assessment. The project 
group met initially weekly and as needed, with 
increasing frequency towards the conference 
dates. Regular coordination and guidance-seeking 
with the Norwegian Chairship team continued 
throughout the planning.

An open invitation for program planning support 
was issued to EPPR Heads of Delegation, and 
regular updates were provided to the Working 
Group throughout the organization of the AEMC. 
The EPPR Expert Group Chairs were invited to 
contribute on their respective thematic areas. The 
established program committee begun its work in 
early June 2024 after some preparatory thematic 
discussions, with further expertise added as the 
program development advanced.

12 ARCTIC EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE 

CONFERENCE CONCEPT NOTE

The Concept Note was developed as an outcome 
of Norwegian stakeholder discussions and it 
outlines the background for the AEMC and the 
visioned format, content, audience and objectives. 
The objective for the conference was as follows:

To provide an inclusive venue for exchanging 
and sharing of information, capacity building, 
discussing the cross-cutting Arctic Council themes 
relevant for emergency prevention, preparedness 
and response, co-production of knowledge 
and learning, as well as for networking and 
establishing and strengthening partnerships. The 
conference applies an approach to emergency 
PPR encompassing all types of risks and hazards 
in the Arctic region.

See AEMC Concept note as Annex 1.

Photo credit Jessica Cook/Arctic Council Secretariat

COMMUNICATION STRATEGY 

The Communication Strategy for the conference 
was developed by Arctic Council Secretariat’s 
PR Officer in cooperation with the EPPR 
Executive Secretary and the EPPR Chair. The 
communications strategy for the conference 
included components from visual branding to 
concrete communications objectives and products 
and guided the outreach and communications 
efforts throughout the conference from planning 
to execution and follow-up activities.

SAFETY / RISK MANAGEMENT

As a part of the conference planning, potential 
risks and vulnerabilities in the project were 
identified. Based on the mapping, a detailed 
risk- and vulnerability analysis was developed to 
support the organization of the event. 

13

CONFERENCE ORGANIZATION

The logistics planning for the conference started 
in early 2024 with securing accommodation, 
administrative services for handling of the 
reservations and registration fees, and the 
venue. Nord University offered to host the event 
at the Bodø main campus, which was deemed 
as an ideal location, being both in the north, 
emphasizing the cross-cutting goal of diverse 
audience and dialogue with research, and the 
strong focus on emergency preparedness in the 
region and at the university.

Program planning and administrative work 
moved forward parallel and complementary 
to each other, enabling flexibility regarding 
production and logistical needs for the event. 
The program structure consisted of a plenary day 
including the opening ceremony, and two days 
of parallel thematic sessions, two workshops and 
an ongoing poster session with lightning talks. 
Program taking place in the main auditorium was 
streamed over the three days for online attendees, 
as well as recorded and published subsequently 
on Arctic Council platforms.

A production company was hired to manage the 
audiovisual production of the conference and 
for the streaming and recording. Additionally a 
close cooperation with university staff, including 
technical and IT personnel, and the staff at the 
Center for Crisis Management and Collaboration 
– Nordlab was required for the organization and 
execution of the event. Nordlab students that 
signed up as volunteers throughout the event 
supporting parallel sessions, general logistics and 
speakers were a valuable part of the team.

EPPR Executive Secretary provided administrative 
and coordination support and facilitation for 
the planning and execution of the conference, 
managing back-end planning and outreach with 
the EPPR Chair (Project Manager), and supporting 
the program committee. Arctic Council Secretariat 
(ACS) PR Officer supported the Executive 
Secretary, and coordinated communications and 
outreach related work as a part of the project 
group. ACS communications team produced 
visual, PR and outreach materials for the 
conference based on the Norwegian Chairship 
and Arctic Council visual style, including an 
opening video and other audiovisual materials. 
Closer to the event, additional support from the 
ACS team was essential in managing speakers and 
at the event for logistical support.

1.4 EVALUATION METHOD 
The evaluation was based both on conference 
aims and planning project goals. The conference 
participants were asked to assess how the Arctic 
Emergency Management Conference achieved its 
goals. The conference participants provided their 
feedback on sessions, workshops, poster sessions 
and demonstrations. 

As part of the evaluation, participants were 
asked to identify one recommendation they took 
away from the conference regarding improved 
cooperation on emergency preparedness in the 
Arctic.

All presenters delivered speaker information 
forms where they reflected upon how the 
presentation is contributing to the Conference 
goals stated below. 

An evaluation survey was sent to conference 
participants after the event to gather feedback 
on the achievement of the conference's purposes 
and organization. Feedback was gathered through 
a survey using the online tool “Nettskjema”, 
Norway’s securest and most used solution for data 
collection. Participants received a link and a QR 
code to provide feedback. 

77 submissions of feedback were received, 
analyzed and included in this report.

2. EVALUATION OF 
CONFERENCE GOALS

2.1 ACCOMPLISHMENT OF 
CONFERENCE GOALS 

The conference participants were asked to assess how well the Arctic Emergency Management 
Conference achieved its goals. The answers were compiled on a scale from 1 to 5, where one was low 
achievement and five was high achievement. Based on the answers from 77 respondents, most of them 
estimated that the conference achieved all four goals (Figure 1).

2.2.2 PARTICIPANT FEEDBACK 
SUMMARY
Thematic sessions and plenary sessions were well 
received, and the inclusion of Indigenous Peoples 
and their experiences was impactful. Participants 
appreciated the longer breaks for networking 
and the overall high quality of the sessions and 
organization.

There was strong appreciation for the continuity 
and complementarity of the sessions. Attendees 
valued how the thematic structure allowed for 
complementarity of the sessions and connections 
between presentations.

The overall execution of the event was praised as 
very well done. However, a few attendees noted 
the lack of input from U.S. -based contributors, 
attributing this to current circumstances beyond 
the organizers’ control.

19

RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE 
CONFERENCES

Based on participant feedback, several 
recommendations emerged to enhance the 
structure and content of potential future Arctic 
emergency management conferences:

• Broadening of disciplinary representation

Attendees noted the absence of perspectives 
from architecture and engineering, particularly 
regarding post-disaster design and reconstruction 
linked to landscape heritage and resilience. 
Feedback from those who primarily attended 
the Wildland fire sessions indicated a desire for 
more targeted content. Specifically, participants 
expressed interest in a dedicated session focused 
on current and emerging tactics and techniques 
for wildfire response. Another idea brought 
forward was a joint Arctic-Antarctic (polar) 
emergency management focus.

• Continuing to emphasize practical 
preparedness but strengthen academic 
integration

Several participants felt that discussions leaned 
heavily toward educational framing rather than 
actionable strategies. Some attendees suggested 
that additional time for discussion and questions 
would have enhanced the overall experience. 
While the presence of practitioners from 
authorities and rescue services was appreciated, 
some participants expressed a desire for deeper 
engagement with academic research. Integration 
of theoretical insights and practical applications 
would be beneficial.

• Ensuring that presenters properly credit 
Indigenous partners and clarify the origins 
of shared knowledge, and acknowledge 
Indigenous Knowledge sources 

• Targeting outreach beyond the core audience

- There was a sense that many attendees were 
already well-versed in the topics discussed. To 
maximize impact, future events might consider 
outreach strategies that engage stakeholders who 
are less familiar with the issues or who hold 
decision-making power in related sectors.

• Practical recommendations to optimize 
session format

- Shorter presentations with more time allocated 
for discussion and engagement were suggested 
for better interaction. 

- The scheduling of numerous parallel sessions 
was seen as limiting. Participants recommended 
organizing themes to allow cross-disciplinary 
attendance and reduce overlap. 

- The introduction of closed thematic sessions 
could help attendees follow coherent topic 
streams without missing key content. 

- Participants appreciated many breaks to detach 
from presentations, but on the last day when 
many participants depart, sessions should not be 
until afternoon.

2.3 WORKSHOPS

21

2.3.2 PARTICIPANT FEEDBACK 
SUMMARY

The workshops received strong praise from 
participants, with many describing them as 
“amazing” and “spot on.” Participants expressed 
that they gained valuable insights, encountering 
information they might not have accessed 
elsewhere. They noted that the presenters were 
articulate and provided clear, well-structured 
content, and many expressed gratitude for the 
opportunity to learn.
Specific sessions during Indigenous Knowledge 
Mobilization Workshop, such as the case study 
on the disaster in Alaska, were highlighted as 
powerful examples of how cultural context 
and lived experience can inform emergency 
management practices. 

The Arctic Oil Spill Research & Development 
Workshop was also well-received, offering a 
valuable space for brainstorming and initiating 
new research directions. Participants appreciated 
the overall organization and relevance of the 
workshops.

There were several suggestions made to enhance 
future sessions:

• Include more case studies and practitioner 
debriefs. Attendees expressed interest in 
additional real-world and firsthand examples 
from practitioners. There was a call for 
more representation from first responders 
and operational experts to shift discussions 
toward practical preparedness and response 
strategies. Several attendees felt that the focus 
should shift toward actionable strategies and 
practical implementation. 

• Some participants were unable to attend in 
person and recommended making workshops 
accessible via online platforms to broaden 
engagement. 

• Suggestions included clearer thematic 
organization and better guidance for locating 
workshop venues. Clearer balance between 
facilitation and working discussions is 
recommended. 

• Consider closed thematic sessions that could 
help participants follow coherent topic 
streams and engage more deeply.

2.4.2 PARTICIPANT FEEDBACK 
SUMMARY

Participants found the exhibition components — 
including posters, booths, and external activities 
— to be highly informative and well-suited 
to the conference format. The poster displays 
were appreciated for their constant availability, 
allowing attendees to engage with the content 
at their own pace. The explanation sessions and 
lightning chats were also valued, though some 
suggested a more structured format to enhance 
clarity and interaction.

Participants appreciated the continuous 
availability of the poster displays, which allowed 
ample time for in-depth reading and reflection. 
The lightning talks were also well-received, with 
attendees noting that having them accessible 
throughout the event enabled thoughtful 
engagement without time pressure. The lightnings 
talks accompanying these exhibits were described 
as interesting and valuable, contributing to a 
richer understanding of the presented material.

Attendees expressed strong appreciation for the 
content showcased in both the poster area and the 
exhibition booths. The displays were described 
as informative and engaging, with several 
participants noting a clear interest in expanding 
industry involvement within the booth area.

The visit to the Norwegian Coast Guard vessel KV 
Bison was highlighted as a particularly engaging 
experience. Attendees appreciated the opportunity 
to step outside the conference setting and interact 
directly with professionals in the field.

RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE 
CONFERENCES

Based on participant input, the following 
recommendations are proposed to enhance future 
exhibition and engagement components:

• Include a brief introduction to poster 
presentations during plenary sessions to 
increase visibility and participation. Create 
more program slots for lightning chats to 
facilitate better engagement.

• Increase the number of posters and booths, 
with more involvement from industry 
stakeholders.

• Provide clear directions to exhibition areas 
and special activities, including external 
venues. Reconfigure poster arrangements to 
allow more space for viewing, such as using 
dual rows or wider aisles.

• In support of remote participation, increase 
the number of posters and booths, with more 
involvement from industry stakeholders.

25

3. EVALUATION OF 
THE CONFERENCE 
PLANNING PROJECT 
GOALS

3.1 “CONDUCT A WELL-ORGANIZED CONFERENCE 
IN 2025 WITH 250 PARTICIPANTS WITH PUBLIC 
SECTOR REPRESENTATIVES, INDIGENOUS PEOPLES 
OF THE ARCTIC, ACADEMIA, INDUSTRY AND OTHER 
RELEVANT ORGANIZATIONS”

The number of participants, including on-site 
and online, was around 330. The backgrounds 
included a broad spectrum from public sector 
representatives, Indigenous Peoples of the Arctic 
and academia to industry and other relevant 
organizations and stakeholders. 

The participants were asked to assess how well 
the conference was organized. The scale ranged 
from 1 (not good at all) to 5 (the best). The 
answers demonstrate a high level of satisfaction 
with the conference organization (Figure 14). 

26 ARCTIC EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE 

Figure 14 Evaluation of the conference organization

In the conference feedback, several 
attendees expressed that this was 
the most impactful emergency 
management conference they had 
experienced throughout their 
professional careers. They noted that 
the event’s focus was exceptionally 
well-aligned with current challenges 
and opportunities in the field. Many 
conveyed their appreciation for what 
they described as an outstanding and 
memorable experience.

Feedback from participants encouraged future 
conferences to further develop formats that 
serve diverse professional needs and foster 
more inclusive, actionable dialogue. Several 
attendees emphasized the importance of inviting 
more operational professionals who are already 
confronting these challenges firsthand. They 
called for improved collaboration and knowledge 
sharing between first responders, scientists, policy 
makers, and city planners.

Participants expressed overall satisfaction with 
the conference, noting that it was well organized 
and ran smoothly. The plenary and thematic 
sessions were described as engaging and 
informative. Opportunities for social interaction 
were appreciated, and the significant involvement 
of Indigenous Peoples was highlighted as a 
meaningful and valued aspect of the event. The 
longer breaks were particularly appreciated, as 
they provided valuable opportunities for meetings 
and networking. Sessions were described as 
engaging and high-quality, and several attendees 
extended their congratulations to the organizers 
for delivering a successful and impactful event.

The AEMC also evaluated the participants’ 
satisfaction with the conference university 
venue. The participants answered from 1 (didn’t 
like at all) to 5 (liked very much). The majority 
appreciated the university venue for the 
conference (Figure 15).

4. RECOMMENDATIONS 
BY THE PARTICIPANTS
The recommendations in this section have been synthesized from the feedback received through the 
evaluation form, and the quotes have been lifted from the evaluation form content.

4.1 STRENGTHENING COOPERATION 
ON EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS AND 
SAFE SHIPPING IN THE ARCTIC

“International cooperation between nations in the circumpolar world can 
make a big difference.”

• Participants emphasized the need 
for improved information sharing on 
resources and communication between 
rescue authorities and local communities. 
Strengthening existing infrastructure and 
knowledge bases was seen as essential, 
particularly in maritime regions where 
expanding industry and services are critical. 

• Some respondents emphasized that Arctic 
cooperation must be prepared to expand once 
geopolitical tensions are resolved. 

• The importance of protecting undersea cables 
was highlighted as a major concern for safe 
shipping and connectivity. 

• There was also a call to continue including 
more high-level emergency management 
practitioners across the Arctic to convene and 
develop harmonized policies from the ground 
up, ensuring consensus and operational 
relevance. 

• Building and maintaining relationships 
was viewed as the foundation for effective 
cooperation, with international conferences 
playing a vital role in fostering mutual 
understanding and sharing best practices.

4.2 DEVELOPING ARCTIC 
COOPERATION ON AERONAUTICAL 
AND MARITIME SEARCH AND

• Feedback underscored the importance of 
continued joint planning and exercises in 
areas such as search and rescue, oil spill 
response and preparedness, radiological 
and nuclear preparedness, and health 
preparedness systems. According to 
participants, the outcomes of the conference 
laid a strong foundation for future 
collaboration and strategic development. 

• Participants advocated for more joint research 
and development initiatives that combine 
academic insight with practitioner experience. 
The need to include academia proactively in 
SAR development was emphasized. 

• Respondents also noted the importance of 
preparing for SAR operations in conflict 
scenarios and ensuring rapid response times 
through improved coordination and resource 
deployment. 

• Participants stressed that preparedness must 
be rooted in realistic assessments of survival 
time and decreasing response times.

4.3 IDENTIFYING ACTIONS TO 
DEAL WITH THE ENVIRONMENTAL 
PROBLEMS ASSOCIATED WITH 
EXPANDING HUMAN ACTIVITY.

“Less is, in the case of Arctic, a lot more.”

• Participants voiced concern over the 
environmental impact of expanding human 
activity in the Arctic. They challenged the 
notion that the region is becoming more 
accessible and open for use, warning that 
such perceptions could promote harmful 
exploitation and result in lasting ecological 
damage. The need to restrict development and 
safeguard the Arctic was emphasized. 

• Some called to broaden the definition of 
emergencies to include environmental and 
cultural dimensions. It is also important to 
incorporate climate change thinking into 
preparedness planning. 

• Expanding community planning with 
lower costs— including health, food, and 
telecommunications — was also seen as 
necessary.

4.4 STRENGTHENING THE 
PREPAREDNESS AND COOPERATION 
WITH ARCTIC INDIGENOUS PEOPLES 
AND ARCTIC COMMUNITIES FOR ALL 
TYPES OF EMERGENCIES, INCLUDING 
WILDLAND FIRES IN ARCTIC BY

AND INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE

• A central theme throughout the feedback was 
the importance of meaningful cooperation 
with Indigenous Peoples and Arctic 
communities. Participants called for the 
integration of the United Nations Declaration 
on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) 
into evacuation policies and emergency 
planning, raising awareness of these 
frameworks among Arctic communities. 

• Indigenous leadership in emergency 
response was strongly advocated, with 
emphasis on listening to Indigenous voices 
and incorporating Traditional Knowledge 
into all stages of emergency planning and 
preparedness. 

• Respondents highlighted the need to include 
Indigenous Peoples and Arctic communities 
in the work that leads to defining emergencies 
and shaping preparedness and declaration of 
an emergency strategies. 

• Building networks, maintaining dialogue, 
learning from each other’s experiences and 
translating these discussions into actionable 
projects were seen as key steps toward 
inclusive and effective cooperation. 

• Participants also noted that Western 
approaches to wildland fire management 
often prioritize saving structures during 
wildfires; however, native populations are 
often more concerned about landscapes 
linked to and providing livelihoods — a 
perspective that should be respected and 
integrated. 

• Enhanced communication capabilities 
across organizations were seen as essential, 
particularly for coordinating responses and 
sharing resources like wildland firefighters 
across borders.

35

5. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS 
BY THE ORGANIZING TEAM
This chapter is not meant to act as a 
comprehensive evaluation of the conference by 
the project team, but to highlight a few key take-
aways to offer food for thought for potential next 
iterations of a similar event.

• Engaging relevant selection of partners and 
expertise, and sufficient resources from the 
beginning, to ensure co-development of the 
program and engagement.

• Securing adequate funding as the planning 
and execution of multidisciplinary conference 
is a lengthy and time-consuming process.

• Supporting Permanent Participant 
engagement in the program planning and in 
leading roles in designing the conference from 
the beginning of the process.

• Reserving time for a process of mapping 
overlap and connecting thematic areas to 
interact within the program is important, as in 
emergency management complex issues are 
interconnected, which should be considered 
in the designing of the event.

• Considering engaging partners that ensure 
a diverse reach including practitioners, 
knowledge holders, researchers, policy 
makers and Arctic and Indigenous 
communities.

• Preparing to unexpected changes: As program 
development was done on a voluntary basis 
by EPPR experts, engagement was affected 
by competing priorities and external factors, 
making fluctuating workload and predicting 
workload challenging – a lot of flexibility is 
needed by the main planners.

• Securing resources early in the planning 
for the use of professional services such as 
production and logistics is recommended, 
especially in hybrid setting including both in-
person and online participation.

The positive feedback received for the AEMC 
shows a clear need for this type of platform 
and the organizers recommend considering the 
inclusion of AEMC or similar conferences with 
Arctic Emergency Management focus on EPPR’s 
work program as appropriate and relevant, with 
further considerations to be taken on a decision-
making level of the Working Group.

CONCEPT NOTE

INTRODUCTION

Norwegian Chairship program for Arctic Council 
2023-2025 states that “We will use concrete 
initiatives and exercises to further develop 
Arctic cooperation on aeronautical and maritime 
search and rescue, oil spill preparedness and 
response, dealing with radiological and nuclear 
contamination at sea, and health preparedness. 
We will also consider the possibility of holding 
an Arctic conference on emergency preparedness 
during our Chairship.”

The mention of the conference in the program 
came through stakeholder consultations by input 
provided by Norwegian EPPR delegation. The 
program also notes an ambition to strengthen 
cooperation with the Arctic Coast Guard Forum, 
which Norway is also chairing during the same 
period.

While on international fora conferences 
within the thematic areas of Arctic emergency 
response do exist and have been arranged by 
multiple stakeholders throughout past years, 
a comprehensive venue dedicated to a holistic 
view of current Arctic emergency landscape 
has been missing. A conference could provide a 
platform for discussions, information exchange 
and to advance work as well as highlight the 
importance and interconnectedness of different 
aspects of emergency prevention, preparedness 

and response in the Arctic. As Arctic inhabitants, 
especially Indigenous Peoples, face the effects and 
risks posed by the changing environment, better 
understanding, capacity building and cooperation 
on all levels from local to global have to be 
strengthened.

Emergencies in the Arctic are a growing concern. 
On top of known circumstances such as vast 
distances, scarce infrastructure and resources 
and sometimes challenging environment and 
weather, affecting and complicating emergency 
preparedness and response, emerging risks in 
the region add to the complexity and frequency 
of possible incidents and disasters. Community 
safety and preparedness, as well as social 
resilience are essential parts of prevention 
of emergencies and enhanced cooperation is 
needed for acknowledging the hazards and for 
informed decision making and actions. Changing 
environment may lead to increased activities thus 
increasing also risks in the region. Prevention 
and preparedness, as well as knowledge-based 
response in emergencies contribute to both 
safeguarding the sensitive environment and 
protecting lives, livelihoods and cultures.

Past Arctic Council Chairmanships have hosted 
thematic events tied to Working Group processes 
and themes, such as CAFF Biodiversity Congress,

could be used as a starting point for planning 
an emergency prevention, preparedness 
and response themed conference during the
